name: Dataverge

profile.reading:
Dataverge operates a data center at 882 3rd Avenue in Brooklyn's Industry City complex, a large waterfront campus in Sunset Park that was built in the early twentieth century as an industrial and warehousing hub and has since been redeveloped into a mixed use complex of offices, manufacturing, retail, and technology tenants. Dataverge markets its space there as the only carrier neutral data center in Brooklyn, a claim tied to the borough's relative scarcity of large scale, multi carrier colocation facilities compared with Manhattan and northern New Jersey.

The facility totals 50,000 square feet, of which 40,000 square feet is raised technical floor, with another 35,000 square feet identified by the operator as available for future expansion within the Industry City campus. Dataverge offers colocation at several scales, from shared racks and locking cabinets up to dedicated cages and private suites, and it markets support for cabinets north of 100 kilowatts for high density and artificial intelligence workloads, a power density well above a typical enterprise colocation deployment. Electrical service reaches the building via two separate utility grids feeding an on site substation rated at 140 megawatts, a campus level utility connection shared across Industry City rather than a figure specific to Dataverge's own IT load. Backup power for the data center itself is provided by 1.75 megawatts of diesel generation, supported by a 3,000 gallon main fuel tank and standing fuel resupply contracts.

Cooling is delivered through a raised floor down flow air system with N plus one redundancy, with the facility held to roughly 75 degrees Fahrenheit and 45 percent relative humidity, both with defined tolerance bands. Security includes multi stage biometric access control and continuous on site monitoring. On the networking side, Dataverge advertises more than forty carriers and providers present in the building, including AT&T, Verizon, Charter, Cogent, Lumen, and Crown Castle, along with direct connections to Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, positioning the facility as a cloud on ramp for customers in the New York City area.

Dataverge's own materials do not state a total IT power capacity in megawatts for the facility or give an opening date, so those figures are recorded here as unpublished rather than assumed.
profile.research_note: Per operator's own facility page: 50,000 sqft total, 40,000 sqft raised floor, 35,000 sqft available for expansion, 1.75MW diesel generator backup (standby, not IT capacity). Two utility grids to an on-site 140MW substation (utility feed, excluded). No IT capacity figure published.

reading:
DataVerge is a privately held, carrier neutral colocation and interconnection operator founded in 2003 and based in Brooklyn. It is a small company by the standards of this registry, and it is here because of where it sits rather than how much power it draws. Its facility occupies space at 882 Third Avenue inside Industry City, the sixteen building, thirty five acre complex in Sunset Park that was built as the Bush Terminal shipping and warehousing yard and has since been reworked into a mixed commercial campus housing several hundred tenants. The registry holds one row for the company, and the stored coordinates land inside the Industry City block, which matches the address on the underlying map tags.

In January 2024 DataVerge signed a twenty year renewal of its lease at Industry City and was named the campus connectivity partner, a formal arrangement in which it supplies fiber, transport, colocation and cloud access to the other tenants of the complex rather than only to its own customers. Reporting on that renewal put the company's occupied space at 50,000 square feet across two floors, with a further 35,000 square feet immediately available and additional empty floors in the building beyond that. DataVerge runs more than five miles of fiber through the campus and connects roughly thirty carriers and network providers. It describes its meet me room as the only carrier neutral one in the borough, which is a claim about Brooklyn specifically and not about New York City, where Manhattan carrier hotels dominate. The company also keeps a secondary site at 111 Town Square Place in Jersey City that it offers for backup and disaster recovery, giving tri state customers a second address without leaving the metro.

The power picture at this site needs care. Industry City has a Con Edison substation on the campus rated at 50 megawatts, and reporting on the lease renewal described DataVerge as the largest user of it with roughly 45 megawatts of capacity available. Those are utility figures, the electricity the campus and its largest tenant can draw, and they are not a statement of critical IT load. DataVerge has not published an IT capacity, a UPS rating or a standby generator count, and older directory entries that circulate a figure of around three megawatts for the site are unattributed and do not say which of those things they are describing. A registry reader should treat the 45 megawatt number as headroom on a shared campus substation rather than as installed computing capacity.

What the company does publish is operational rather than electrical. It states a 99.999 percent uptime commitment, round the clock on site technical staff, and SOC 1 SSAE 18 Type 2 and PCI compliance, and it names direct connections to the large public clouds alongside its carrier list. Ownership beyond the founders is not disclosed. Ray Sidler is named as chief executive and cofounder, and the company traces its corporate lineage through earlier entities before settling on the DataVerge name. It reports that it owns and operates its own infrastructure, though it leases the building space rather than owning it, which the twenty year lease term makes explicit.

The useful way to read this record is as an outer borough interconnection point rather than a compute site. Its value to customers is the fiber and the meet me room in a borough of two and a half million people that otherwise routes through Manhattan, not density of racks.
